extracted.intended_audience: patent prosecutors and practitioners drafting AI-related patent applications (patent attorneys, in-house counsel, inventors)
extracted.subtask_description: Best-practice guidance for drafting and claiming AI inventions to survive eligibility (35 U.S.C. §101/Alice), enablement (§112), and prior art scrutiny; focuses on claim/content framing, disclosures, and filing strategy across jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame the Invention as a Technical Improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-Alice, AI patents need a clear technical-improvement narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give concrete technical improvements as the core of the invention (examples: a new model architecture that reduces inference latency; a new training procedure that uses less memory; a new data augmentation strategy that improves robustness; a new neural network module specialized for a domain). Emphasize how the AI changes or improves a technical process or system rather than presenting abstract functionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Pure Math Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite only mathematical operations without anchoring to a technical use case are textbook abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor every AI claim to (a) what the model does in operational terms, (b) what hardware/system it runs on, and (c) what technical improvement it provides. Avoid claims that merely recite matrix multiplications, activation functions, or other raw math.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose the Model Architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification should disclose the model architecture sufficiently that a POSITA could reproduce it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not full source code, but include layer counts, layer types (conv, attention, MLP), connection patterns, hyperparameter ranges, and training data characteristics. Enough technical detail supports enablement and distinguishes over abstract descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recite Specific Architectural Choices in Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should recite concrete architectural elements rather than high-level descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a claim reciting 'a transformer with 12 layers and 768-dimensional embeddings, where attention is computed using a sparse pattern that...' is more eligible than 'a neural network that predicts X.' Specific architecture details buy eligibility and help distinguish prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft Parallel Training-Phase and Inference-Phase Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Different actors may infringe at training time vs. inference time; claims should cover both phases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File parallel claims directed to training methods, trained models, and inference/deployment methods to reach both the entity that trained the model and the entity that runs it (deploys/serves predictions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim the Trained Model as Data
rubrics_metrics.description: A trained model (its parameters) can be claimed as data stored on a medium to reach distribution and use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example claim form: 'a non-transitory computer-readable medium storing model parameters trained according to method X.' Such claims can target model distribution as well as use of the model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose Training Data Characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification should disclose characteristics of the training data rather than simply naming datasets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include size, modality, label distribution, augmentation strategy, and other characteristics. Training data choices can be inventive and therefore support claim limitations; full dataset disclosure is not required but meaningful characteristics should be described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address Enablement/'Black Box' Risks (§112)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that merely state 'a model trained to determine X' may face §112 enablement problems if not reproducible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose the training objective, loss function, and key hyperparameters. Provide sufficient procedural detail about training to avoid enablement rejections when outcomes depend on training choices or stochastic factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft for Federated and Distributed Training with Single-Actor Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For federated or distributed learning, structure claims to reflect enforceable single-actor steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft method claims with single-actor architecture: have the orchestrator perform the steps that combine data even if underlying gradients come from multiple clients. This helps avoid multi-actor/non-infringement issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider Foreign Filing Regimes and Tailor the Spec
rubrics_metrics.description: Different patent offices treat AI differently; tailor disclosures and claim framing for target jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPO is generally more favorable to AI patents than USPTO post-Alice; CNIPA has its own AI-specific guidance. Support both 'technical improvement' framing (US/EPO) and the EPO-specific 'further technical effect' framework when drafting to multiple jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigate Open-Source Foundation Model Risk
rubrics_metrics.description: If the base model architecture is open-source, claims must focus on the inventive additions rather than the unmodified foundation model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the foundational model (e.g., a Llama variant) is open-source, draft claims on what the inventor added: the fine-tuning data, the prompt strategy, the post-processing, the system architecture. Claims reading on an unmodified foundation model are likely anticipated.
